rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast scouting gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the crowded central cluster and nearly coeluting final pair. The short initial elution window leaves ample time to use a shallower gradient afterward if needed.

Test a substantially shallower gradient at the better-performing temperature to spread the central cluster and assess slope-dependent selectivity. The current last peak at 4.71 minutes provides room to improve resolution without necessarily incurring a time penalty.

The shallower gradient resolves the central cluster, leaving just one critical pair. Lower temperature by one step to shift that pair’s selectivity while retaining the favorable gradient and sub-10-minute elution window.

At 60 C, an intermediate gradient duration may separate the later pair that converged at 24 minutes while preserving enough resolution in the central cluster. This also reduces the last-peak time relative to the current best method.

This gives a gradient slope between the original 18- and 20-minute equivalents, targeting improved separation of the late critical pair while keeping both central pairs above 1.5. It should also bring the last peak out slightly earlier than injection 5.

Increase the slope slightly from 0.04444 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute, targeting R ≥ 1.5 for the remaining critical pair while preserving central-pair resolution. The final peak should elute before the gradient ends, so the lower endpoint should not affect its elution.

Injection 7 achieves the maximum CRF; now test a slightly steeper gradient to seek an earlier last peak while retaining full resolution. The central pairs have little margin, so this small slope increase probes the speed limit while preserving injection 7 as the best method.

The steeper-gradient test reached the central-pair resolution limit, so retain injection 7’s slope and raise the starting organic fraction by one step. This tests whether shifting the gradient window can shorten elution while maintaining full resolution; injection 7 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Make the gradient shallower to recover central-cluster resolution lost when raising the starting organic fraction. This tests whether the higher-starting window can still deliver full resolution with an earlier last peak than injection 7.

The high-temperature refinements show opposing resolution limits, so explore low-temperature selectivity for a different fully resolved solution. A higher starting fraction and moderately steeper gradient should help offset increased retention; injection 7 remains the maximum-CRF fallback.

Shorten the low-temperature gradient to test whether slope-dependent selectivity opens the sole unresolved central pair while reducing elution time. Watch the later pair at R 1.65, which has limited margin for compression.

Raise temperature one step at the faster low-temperature gradient to test whether selectivity can resolve the central pair and improve the marginal later pair. This explores a potentially shorter fully resolved method while retaining injection 7 as the maximum-score fallback.

Test a lower starting organic fraction to strengthen central-cluster separation, paired with a steeper gradient to offset the added retention. This may allow a shorter fully resolved run than injection 7, which remains the maximum-score reference.

Slightly reduce the slope from injection 14 to improve both marginal central separations while monitoring the opposing trend in the later pairs. This tests a potentially more robust maximum-score alternative to injection 7, with all peaks still expected before 10 minutes.

Test a higher starting fraction with a compensating shallower gradient to recover central-pair resolution while shortening the elution window. Injection 7 already achieves the maximum CRF and remains the fallback if this alternative loses resolution.

Test a narrower gradient followed by a hold: the slightly shallower slope should preserve central-cluster resolution, while the hold may improve selectivity among later peaks. Injection 7 remains the established maximum-score method; this run probes an alternative rather than a higher possible CRF.

Shift the low-temperature gradient window upward while retaining injection 11’s slope, testing starting-composition selectivity against its unresolved central pair. This may shorten retention substantially; injection 7 remains the confirmed maximum-score method.

Raise the starting fraction another step while preserving the slope to extend the selectivity shift seen in injection 18 and shorten retention. The central pair is the only unresolved pair, while the later pair at R 1.66 needs monitoring.

Continue the upward window shift at the same slope: the previous step markedly improved the critical central pair and shortened elution. This could achieve full resolution substantially faster than injection 7, though the neighboring central gap may narrow.

Injection 20 gives full resolution with the last peak at 4.14 minutes; shorten the gradient one step to seek a faster maximum-score method. Monitor the central and later pairs at R 1.61 and 1.65, retaining injection 20 if either drops below 1.5.

Test a slope between injections 20 and 21 to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary more closely. Injection 20 remains the preferred confirmed method, with maximum CRF and the last peak at 4.14 minutes.

Test a slightly lower starting fraction to restore the limiting central gap, combined with higher temperature and a steeper gradient to accelerate elution. This probes a different selectivity balance near the fast optimum while retaining injection 20 as the shortest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test one higher starting-organic step with a substantially shallower gradient to compensate for compression of the limiting central pair. This explores whether the elution window can be shortened further while retaining injection 20 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Preserve injection 20’s successful starting composition, slope, and temperature while shortening the programmed gradient to four minutes. Its outlet gradient ends at 4.65 minutes, after the observed last peak at 4.14 minutes, so full resolution and maximum CRF should be retained.
